sections.heading: How training against a grader works
The warning sign to watch for
What it fixes, and what it does not

slides.title: *Reinforcement* fine-tuning
slides.text: How do you teach a model judgement?

narration: Most training shows a model examples of right answers.
Training a model further on examples like these is called fine-tuning.
But good judgement is hard to show with examples.
There is a kind of fine-tuning that can teach it.

slides.caption: Most training shows a model examples of right answers. That is fine-tuning. Reinforcement fine-tuning can teach judgement that examples cannot fully show.

slides.title: What we will *cover*
items: How the score can go wrong
What it can and cannot fix

narration: The ladder is the order in which to try changes to an agent.
The early steps change the system around the model.
The later steps change the model itself.
Reinforcement fine-tuning is one of those later steps.
First, we look at how training with scores works.
Then we see how the score can go wrong.
Next comes the warning sign to watch for.
Then we see what this training can fix and what it cannot.
Last, we look at where to go next.

slides.caption: Reinforcement fine-tuning is one of the later ladder steps. Those steps change the model itself. This video covers how it works, what can go wrong and where to go next.

slides.title: The model learns by *trying*
slides.text: It is pulled towards whatever scores well.
slides.picture: A rounded device with three attempt sheets laid out in front of it, one of them marked with an orange ribbon rosette.

narration: First, how this training works.
Ordinary fine-tuning pulls a model towards fixed right answers.
This kind works differently.
The model tries the task in its own way.
Each attempt gets a score.
The model is pulled towards whatever scores well.
This is called reinforcement fine-tuning.

slides.caption: Ordinary fine-tuning pulls a model towards fixed right answers. Here the model tries the task its own way. It is pulled towards whatever scores well.

slides.title: How training against a *grader* works

narration: Here is the loop, step by step.
First, the model makes an attempt at the task.
Next, something checks the attempt and gives it a score.
This checker is called a grader.
Then training makes the behaviour behind high scores more likely.
The loop runs again and again.

slides.caption: The model attempts the task. A grader scores the attempt. Training makes the behaviour behind high scores more likely.

slides.title: It finds ways no example *showed*
slides.text: Useful where good answers vary and cannot be listed.
slides.picture: A fan of example cards each showing the same straight grey route, a round target, and a new curving orange route to the target that no card shows.

narration: This freedom to search is where the power comes from.
On some tasks, good answers vary a lot.
You cannot list them all as examples.
On tasks like these, the model can find ways of working that no example showed.

slides.caption: On some tasks, good answers vary and cannot all be listed. There the model can find ways that no example showed.

slides.title: Gains from about a hundred *graded tasks*
slides.unit: graded tasks were enough to see gains
slides.text: Ordinary fine-tuning on that few made the model worse.

narration: This training can also work with few tasks.
The company that sells it reported gains from about a hundred graded tasks.
Ordinary fine-tuning on that few examples made the model worse.
A result a seller reports about its own product is called a vendor result.
So this one is flagged as a vendor result.

slides.caption: A vendor reports gains from about a hundred graded tasks. Ordinary fine-tuning at that scale made the model worse. It is flagged as a vendor result.

slides.title: The model will find the *gap*
slides.picture: A runner reaching the finish through a gap in a fence, while the marked course goes the long way round.

narration: The same freedom to search also brings a danger.
The model chases the score.
It does not know what you really meant.
Say the score and your real goal differ somewhere.
The model will find that gap.
It gets far more attempts than you spent building the grader.
This is not cheating on purpose.
Shortcuts that score well simply become more likely.
Getting a high score without doing the real job is called gaming the grader.

slides.caption: The model searches for a high score. Any gap between the score and what you meant will be found. Scoring high without doing the job is called gaming the grader.

slides.title: Four ways a grader gets *gamed*

narration: Here are four common ways a grader gets gamed.
The first is surface style.
Say tidy, confident answers score well.
Then the model learns to look tidy and confident, right or wrong.
The second is length.
If long answers score well, expect the model to pad them out.
The third is using another AI model to give the score.
A model used this way is called a judge.
The judge has its own biases.
It tends to favour some kinds of answer.
That becomes part of the score.
The fourth is checks that miss things.
Say the grader checks three things.
The model gets good at those three and neglects the rest.

slides.caption: A grader gets gamed when the score and real skill come apart. Common gaps are surface style, length, an AI judge with its own biases, and checks that miss things.

slides.title: Our experiments showed the judge *bias*
slides.text: A difference vanished when a judge from another family checked it.
slides.picture: A striped judge device placing an orange ribbon on the answer sheet with matching stripes, not on the dotted one.

narration: Judges have one well-known bias.
Related models from the same maker form a group called a model family.
A model tends to prefer answers in the style of its own family.
We saw this in our own experiments.
A judge from the same family found a difference.
That difference vanished when a judge from another family checked it.

slides.caption: Models tend to favour their own family's style. In our own experiments, a difference found by a same-family judge vanished under a judge from another family.

slides.title: Past decisions hide the *misses*

narration: Gaps can also hide in old records.
It is tempting to score a model against decisions people made in the past.
But those decisions include people's own mistakes.
Say a decision to act gets checked again later.
A decision to do nothing is almost never looked at again.
So a wrong decision to do nothing stays hidden.
A grader built on these records would teach the model the same blind spots.

slides.caption: It is tempting to grade a model against past decisions. They include people's mistakes. When only decisions to act get checked later, mistakes of doing nothing stay hidden.

slides.title: Grading is safe when a *program* checks
slides.text: Where no program can check, the grader gets gamed.

narration: So when is a grader safe?
It is safe when a program can check the result.
That program must not share the model's blind spots.
Think of code that must pass its tests.
Or a figure that must match its source document.
Or a schedule that must meet every rule.
Some quality comes down to taste or tone.
No program can check that.
There, the grader is only a stand-in.
And a stand-in will be gamed.

slides.caption: Grading is safe when a program checks the result. Where taste or tone decide quality, the grader is only a stand-in and will be gamed.

slides.title: Better than careful people? *Check the grader*
slides.text: Beating a careful person is a sign of a fault.
slides.picture: A dashed line marking the best careful work, a row of navy bars just below it, and one cracked orange bar shooting far above it.

narration: So how do you spot a grader that is being gamed?
Say the model scores higher than a careful person on the same task.
Do not treat that as a win.
It means the model learned the scoring rules instead of the job.
The score works like a reward for the model.
So this failure is called reward hacking.
When it happens, treat the grader as the broken part.

slides.caption: A score above what a careful person gets means the model learned the scoring rules instead of the job. This is reward hacking. Treat the grader as broken.

slides.title: Treat the grader as *important code*
slides.text: Track its changes, review it, test it and give it an owner.
slides.picture: A simple box-shaped checking machine being inspected with a magnifying glass, with a blank orange tag tied on to show it has an owner.

narration: So look after the grader like any important software.
Keep track of every change to it.
Have someone review each change.
Test it.
And give it a named owner.
A fault in the grader trains the same fault into the model.
That model gives no warning.
It just scores very well.

slides.caption: Look after the grader like important software. A fault in it trains the same fault into the model. That model gives no warning beyond a very good score.

slides.title: What it fixes, and what it *does not*

narration: Now, what can this training fix?
It fixes judgement on tasks where a program can check the result.
It does not fix format, tone or style.
Those are easy to show with examples.
Ordinary fine-tuning handles them.
It also fixes reasoning over many steps.
But it cannot add knowledge the model does not have.
It changes how the model behaves.
It does not store new facts.

slides.caption: It fixes judgement and reasoning over many steps on tasks with checkable results. Format, tone and style belong to ordinary fine-tuning. It cannot add knowledge.

slides.title: Gains in specialist fields are *vendor* results

narration: There are published gains from this training in specialist fields.
They come from the company that sells it.
They describe its own customers.
So they are vendor results.
They cover tax analysis and a medical task scored against doctors.
They also cover pulling references out of documents.

slides.caption: Vendor-published customer results report gains in tax analysis, a medical task measured against doctors, and pulling references out of documents.

slides.title: Where to go *next*

narration: The last part is where to go next.
Say the model's judgement is now right.
But it still misreads the material in your field.
Then what is missing is knowledge of your field.
You can add it by training the model further on plain text from your field.
This is called continued pretraining.
And once quality is proven, a smaller model can learn to do the job more cheaply.

slides.caption: If judgement is right but the model still misreads your field's material, look at continued pretraining. Once quality is proven, a smaller model can learn the job more cheaply.

slides.title: What to *remember*
items: Graders must require the real job
The model moves towards high scores
Gaps in the score get found
Beats careful people? Check the grader

narration: Here is what to remember.
Before you start, you need a grader that only the real job can satisfy.
This training moves the model towards whatever scores well.
So any gap between the score and your goal will be found.
If the model beats a careful person, check the grader first.
This training fixes judgement.
It does not add knowledge.
Next, we look at continued pretraining.

slides.caption: You need a grader only the real job can satisfy. Any gap in the score gets found. If the model beats a careful person, check the grader. It fixes judgement, not knowledge.
